config.title: React Server Components & SSR vs SSG

intro.title: React Server Components & SSR vs SSG
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple blog page that displays a list of posts to understand how React renders content. You will learn the core concepts of Server-Side Rendering (SSR) and Static Site Generation (SSG), which determine when and where your React components are rendered. The main technologies involved are React, TypeScript, and Next.js, which provides built-in support for these rendering methods. By the end, you'll know how to choose between SSR for dynamic content and SSG for faster, pre-built pages, all while writing type-safe code with TypeScript.
intro.usecase: React Server Components and SSR/SSG patterns are essential for building performant content-heavy applications like e-commerce product pages, news websites, and documentation portals. For example, an e-commerce site uses SSR to render product listings with real-time inventory data, while SSG pre-builds static product detail pages for better SEO and faster loading. A news platform might use Server Components to fetch and render articles without sending JavaScript to the client, improving initial page load. These patterns help developers optimize performance by reducing client-side JavaScript and delivering content faster to users.

objectives: Apply React Server Components to render static content without client-side JavaScript
Implement Server-Side Rendering (SSR) to generate HTML on each request using Next.js
Utilize Static Site Generation (SSG) to pre-render pages at build time for performance
Construct a Next.js page component that uses the 'use client' directive for client interactivity
Define and export a getServerSideProps function to implement SSR data fetching
Execute getStaticProps to fetch data at build time for SSG pages
Compare SSR and SSG implementations by applying different data fetching strategies
Use the 'async' keyword to handle asynchronous operations in server components
Control component rendering location by assigning 'use client' or leaving components as server components
Access server-side data directly in server components without useEffect or useState hooks
Modify Next.js configuration to adjust caching behavior for SSR and SSG pages
Return appropriate props from data fetching functions to hydrate page components with data

steps.title: Import React and ReactDOM from 'react' and 'react-dom/server'
steps.instruction: Import React from 'react' and ReactDOM from 'react-dom/server'.
steps.hint: Use the import keyword followed by the package name in quotes.
steps.seedCode:
// Import React from 'react' and ReactDOM from 'react-dom/server' here

// Your component code will go below
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have imported the core React packages needed for server-side rendering.
successCriteria: The code includes two import statements: one for React from 'react' and one for ReactDOM from 'react-dom/server'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and ReactDOM. These are essential for working with React components and server-side rendering.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your import statements. Make sure you're importing React from 'react' and ReactDOM from 'react-dom/server'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to import React from 'react' and ReactDOM from 'react-dom/server' using the import keyword.

steps.title: Create a Server Component function
steps.instruction: Create a ServerComponent function that returns a React element. Use TypeScript syntax and return JSX.
steps.hint: Define a function named ServerComponent that returns a JSX element like a <div>.
steps.expectedOutcome: A ServerComponent function is defined with TypeScript and returns JSX.
successCriteria: The code defines a function named ServerComponent that returns JSX (e.g., a <div>).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a Server Component function with TypeScript.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you define a function named ServerComponent that returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: Please create a function named ServerComponent that returns a JSX element.

steps.title: Add props interface to Server Component
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface for your Server Component's props, then add it to the function's parameter type annotation.
steps.hint: Create an interface with a name like 'ServerComponentProps' and include at least one property (e.g., 'message' of type string). Then update your component function to accept props of that type.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your Server Component will have typed props via a TypeScript interface, making it type-safe.
successCriteria: Interface includes at least one property
Component function signature uses the interface as props type
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined a TypeScript interface for your Server Component props and applied it to the component. This ensures type safety for the data your component receives.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but something's missing. Make sure you've defined an interface with at least one property and used it in your component's parameter type annotation.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to define a TypeScript interface for props and use it in your Server Component function signature.

steps.title: Add server-side data fetching to Server Component
steps.instruction: Inside your ServerComponent function, add an async data fetch using the fetch API. Since this is a Server Component, you can directly call fetch without useEffect.
steps.hint: Use the async keyword on your component function and call fetch inside it. You can fetch from a mock API endpoint like 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1'.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your ServerComponent function should now be async and contain a fetch call to retrieve data from an external API.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added server-side data fetching to your Server Component. This demonstrates how Server Components can directly fetch data without client-side hooks like useEffect.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your component function is marked as async and you're properly using the fetch API with await. Remember to parse the JSON response.
steps.feedbackWrong: This step requires adding an async data fetch inside your ServerComponent. Server Components can directly call fetch without useEffect. Try adding 'async' to your function and using fetch with await.

steps.feedbackPartial:

steps.title: Create a Client Component function
steps.instruction: Create a ClientComponent function that returns a React element. This will be a regular client-side React component for comparison with the ServerComponent.
steps.hint: Define a function named ClientComponent that returns JSX. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: A ClientComponent function is defined that returns a React element.
successCriteria: The code should contain a function named ClientComponent that returns JSX (React element).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a ClientComponent function. This will allow us to compare server and client components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined a function named ClientComponent that returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ClientComponent function is not properly defined. Please create a function named ClientComponent that returns a React element.

steps.title: Add useState hook to Client Component
steps.instruction: Import the useState hook from 'react' and use it to declare a state variable called 'count' initialized to 0 in your ClientComponent function.
steps.hint: Import useState from 'react' and call useState<number>(0) inside the ClientComponent function to create the state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ClientComponent will have the useState hook imported and a 'count' state variable declared.
successCriteria: Declare const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0) inside ClientComponent
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported useState and initialized the count state in your ClientComponent. This demonstrates how client components can manage local state using React hooks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've both imported useState from 'react' AND declared the count state variable with useState<number>(0) inside the ClientComponent function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ClientComponent doesn't have the useState hook properly set up. Remember to import useState from 'react' and use it to create a count state variable initialized to 0.

steps.title: Add useEffect for data fetching in Client Component
steps.instruction: Import the useEffect hook from 'react' and use it inside your ClientComponent to fetch data when the component mounts.
steps.hint: Add the import statement for useEffect, then call useEffect inside your ClientComponent with a callback function that performs the data fetch.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ClientComponent should now include a useEffect hook that will run when the component mounts, ready to fetch data.
successCriteria: Pass an empty dependency array [] as second argument
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the useEffect hook to your ClientComponent. This will allow you to fetch data when the component mounts.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've both imported useEffect and called it inside your ClientComponent with an empty dependency array.
steps.feedbackWrong: This step requires adding the useEffect hook to your ClientComponent. You need to import it from 'react' and call it inside your component.

steps.title: Create SSR rendering function
steps.instruction: Create a function named renderSSR that takes a component and props, and returns the server-rendered HTML string using ReactDOM.renderToString.
steps.hint: Define a function that accepts a component and props, then calls ReactDOM.renderToString with the component rendered with those props.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a renderSSR function that can take a React component and props, and return the server-rendered HTML string.
successCriteria: The function must be named renderSSR, accept a component and props as parameters, and return the result of ReactDOM.renderToString.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created an SSR rendering function that can generate HTML strings from React components on the server.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function: 1) is named renderSSR, 2) accepts both component and props parameters, and 3) returns ReactDOM.renderToString with the component rendered with props.
steps.feedbackWrong: The SSR rendering function is not correctly implemented. Remember to create a function named renderSSR that takes a component and props, then uses ReactDOM.renderToString to render the component with those props.

steps.title: Create SSG rendering function
steps.instruction: Create a function named `renderStatic` that returns a string of HTML by calling `ReactDOM.renderToString()` with a React element. This function should be synchronous (not async) and demonstrate static generation at build time.
steps.hint:
Define a regular function (not async) that returns the result of `ReactDOM.renderToString()`. You can pass a simple JSX element like `
Static Content
` as the argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a synchronous function named `renderStatic` that uses `ReactDOM.renderToString()` to generate static HTML.
successCriteria: Function calls `ReactDOM.renderToString()` with a React element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a static generation function. This demonstrates how components can be pre-rendered at build time to produce static HTML.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function is named `renderStatic`, returns a string, and calls `ReactDOM.renderToString()` with a JSX element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't meet the requirements. Remember to create a synchronous function named `renderStatic` that returns the result of `ReactDOM.renderToString()`.

steps.title: Add comparison display in main component
steps.instruction: Create a new functional component named ComparisonDisplay that returns a JSX structure containing both the ServerComponent and ClientComponent side by side.
steps.hint: Define a new component that renders both existing components within a container element like a <div>.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new component that renders both ServerComponent and ClientComponent for side-by-side comparison.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a comparison component that displays both server and client components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your component renders both ServerComponent and ClientComponent.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should render both ServerComponent and ClientComponent for comparison.

steps.title: Add explanatory comments and console logs
steps.instruction: Add console.log statements and explanatory comments to the ServerComponent, ClientComponent, SSR function, and SSG function to show when each renders.
steps.hint: Add console.log('ServerComponent rendering') inside ServerComponent, console.log('ClientComponent rendering') inside ClientComponent, and similar logs in the SSR and SSG functions. Also add comments explaining the rendering timing differences.
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will include console.log statements in each component/function and comments explaining when they render (server vs client, SSR vs SSG).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added console logs and comments to demonstrate the rendering timing differences between server components, client components, SSR, and SSG.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some console logs or comments, but make sure to add them to all four places: ServerComponent, ClientComponent, SSR function, and SSG function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding console.log statements inside each component/function and add comments explaining when they render (server vs client, SSR vs SSG).
